name: Tomas Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Tomas, 27, and I'm a junior marketing executive at Ironleaf, a sports nutrition brand that sells protein powder and snack bars, mostly online. I live with my girlfriend Lucia, who's a pharmacy technician, and we're saving to get married and buy a place. My older brother Mateo runs a gym across town, which is half the reason I ended up in this industry.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My day is email flows, product launch pages and the ads we run on social media. I use AI tools all day: I've built little automations that write first drafts of product emails and sort customer reviews into themes. I'm not the strongest writer, and my manager Carl still catches lazy lines, but I'm fast and I like building systems. What wears me out is when a launch slips and I have to rewrite everything for a new date at midnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are useful and that's that, no revolution. At work I'd say let's keep what saves time and get back to selling protein. Online I'd post my favourite automations for other small brands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel good about it. I've already built the shortcuts, so I'm ahead of people who waited. Sports nutrition is growing, people keep getting into the gym, and Ironleaf had its best year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building automations and ask Carl for a small raise based on the hours I've saved the team. I'd start a side project helping my brother's gym with its marketing, maybe for a small fee. And I'd keep saving, we're at about four months now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, honestly. A plateau is a world where hard work and a bit of cleverness still pay. I'd be a little bored, but I'd take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask for a raise. What would you say to Carl?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show him a spreadsheet: my email automations save about six hours a week across the team. That's real money. Even a 5 percent raise would help with the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Mateo feel about you doing his gym's marketing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mateo would say yes and then complain about paying me. He'd probably pay me in free membership and dinners. That's family.

I'd post my favourite **automations** to help other small brands.
think: He's **ahead** because he built shortcuts while others waited.
Sports nutrition is **growing**, and Ironleaf had its best year.
do: Ask Carl for a **raise** based on six hours saved weekly.
Do marketing for his **brother's gym** for a small fee.
Keep saving on top of **four months** already put by.
feel: **Pretty good**, in a world where hard work still pays.
A little **bored**, but happy to take it.

fieldNote: He feels **secure**, with a growing brand and tool skills.
He measures his value in **hours saved** and wants paying for it.
**Family** is both his side business and his safety net.

steps.text: Show Carl the hours his email automations save and ask for a raise
Run marketing for his brother Mateo's gym for a small fee
Keep saving toward the wedding and a home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance, not a threat, if you're willing to work. I'd say people should learn the tools instead of waiting for the government to save them. At work I'd offer to lead the switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm okay for now, maybe even better off. But I'm not naive: a junior who mostly writes emails is the easiest thing to cut. I'd need to be the person who builds and runs the systems, not the person who writes the lines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Carl to make me the team's automation lead, with a title change, within six months. I'd learn the analytics side properly, maybe a 400 course. And I'd turn the gym marketing into a small business for three or four local gyms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but fired up. I like a challenge. But I know confidence doesn't pay rent if Ironleaf decides to cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people shouldn't wait for the government. What about people who can't adapt as fast as you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fair. Some people can't, and their families and churches should help them first. I'd help my dad, who's a bus driver, learn whatever he needs. But I don't think a cheque from the state is the answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Ironleaf would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hannah, who does customer service emails. That's exactly what the software takes. I'd try to get her onto my automation team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and people need to move fast. I'd still say families and businesses should lead, but I'd admit some government help would be needed. Online I'd share practical steps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my tool skills buy me maybe a year. If AI can do any thinking work, it doesn't need me to build automations. Ironleaf could run with a few people and a lot of software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go into business with Mateo, building out the gym, because training people is hands-on and robots are three years behind. I'd get a personal training certificate in the first few months. Lucia and I would marry small and quickly, and put the rest into the gym.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, though I'd be moving. Two years is nothing. But I'd rather be running than waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Putting your savings into the gym. Isn't that risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but sitting on four months of savings while my job disappears is risky too. If people lose desk jobs, some of them will have more time for the gym, at least for a while. And Mateo knows the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Lucia think about the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lucia would want to keep some savings back, and she'd be right. We'd agree on putting half in. Her pharmacy job is safer for a bit, but not forever.

I'd admit some **government help** would be needed this time.

steps.text: Put half their savings into his brother Mateo's gym

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to prepare, so let's not waste them. I'd tell young people to learn a trade or a hands-on skill alongside their desk job. At work I'd keep pushing the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have three good years where my automation skills make me valuable, maybe even get promoted. Then it thins. I'd use those years to build something of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Ironleaf and push for promotion, saving hard. By year two I'd do the personal training certificate and start coaching on weekends at Mateo's gym. By 2030 I'd want a part-share in the gym.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a good way, like before a big match. I'd have a plan with dates. I just hope the dates hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want a part-share in the gym. How would you pay for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Savings, plus maybe a small bank loan. My brother Mateo wants to open a second gym anyway. I'd bring the marketing and Mateo would bring the training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the wedding fit in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd marry next year as planned. Lucia's family would want a proper church wedding. I'd save harder rather than cut that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone willing to work. I'd encourage people to start side businesses and learn trades. At work I'd keep leading on the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well for most of the decade. I'd climb at Ironleaf or a bigger brand, then move into the gym business around 2032. Robots for hands-on work come around 2039, so that's a long stretch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building automations and aim for a manager role in three years. I'd save toward a house with Lucia and buy in about two years. I'd do the training certificate around year three and start coaching part-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish. It's a long runway, and I like plans. I'd still think about 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in 2039, when the robots come for the gym too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. Maybe people will still want a human coach shouting at them in 2039. Or maybe I'd have to start again at 40.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you have children by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably two by then. I'd want them to grow up seeing their dad build something. That matters to me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because two years isn't enough to build anything, even for someone who moves fast. What would help is cheap loans for small businesses and short trade courses, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about pride. People like me want to earn our way, and I'd want any help to come as a chance to work, not a cheque.

headlineQuote: People like me want to earn our way, and I'd want any help to come as a chance to work, not a cheque.
portrait: Tomas is a **27-year-old junior marketer** at a sports nutrition brand, living with Lucia, a pharmacy technician.
He uses **AI daily** and builds automations, and moves first.
He sees slow change as a **chance**, but admits juniors who write are easy cuts.
Faster AGI pushes him toward his **brother's gym**, a hands-on bridge.
His values favour **work and family** over state support.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years isn't enough to build anything.
